title: Clamp a round-bottom flask on a lab stand
instruction: Clamp the round-bottom flask by its neck in the lab stand's clamp, so that it hangs there clear of the table, without dropping or tipping it, and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Clamping a round-bottom flask by its neck on a lab stand is a common wet-lab step that chemists and lab technicians do by hand many times a week: it starts nearly every reflux, distillation or stirred reaction. It is done here as in the lab: the flask is lifted by its neck, the neck (below its glass joint, as lab manuals advise) is set in the open clamp with the flask hanging clear, and the flask is let go only once the jaws hold it. This stand carries a spring flask clamp with a release lever on its arm: springs keep its cork-lined jaws shut, and they open only while the lever is held down. So one hand must keep the clamp open while the other brings the fragile flask in, and must let the jaws close before the flask is let go. One hand can't do both: holding the flask, the jaws stay shut and the neck can't get in.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases, sideways from the midpoint between them, and up from the table top. (1) A lab stand at the back left: a 6 x 9 in (15.2 x 22.9 cm) cast-iron base, 1.3 cm thick, its long side running forward, from 27.6 to 50.5 cm forward and from 15.4 to 30.6 cm left, and a zinc-plated steel rod 24 in (61 cm) tall and 1/2 in (12.7 mm) across, at 48 cm forward, 23 cm left. In a real trial the base is held by a C-clamp or a 2 kg weight so it can't shift (fixed in the simulation). (2) Two stainless boss heads (3 cm): one on the rod holds a 1/2 x 12 in (12.7 mm x 30.5 cm) steel support rod as a crossbar, running forward at 7 cm up from 55.5 to 25 cm forward, 23 cm left; the other, at 28 cm forward, holds the clamp's arm 2.5 cm above the crossbar. (3) The clamp, built to the drawing in the code archive: its arm, a 1/2 in aluminium tube, runs from that boss head toward the centre line at 28 cm forward, 9.5 cm up, into the clamp head (aluminium, 15 cm long (running forward), 3 cm deep, 1.6 cm tall), whose front face, 2 cm left of the centre line, stops the neck. Two jaws close on the clamp's middle line (28 cm forward) from in front and behind, each a cork pad 6 mm thick, 4 cm long (from 2.2 cm right to 1.8 cm left of the centre line) and 1.6 cm tall on an 8 mm aluminium arm, 9.5 cm up. A spring per jaw (0.25 N/mm, 3.0 N preload) keeps them shut, 2 mm apart. (4) The clamp's lever: a red aluminium bar pivoted on the arm 12 cm left of the centre line, 12 cm up, running toward the stand, 2.25 cm forward of the arm's line, with a black rubber pad 2.5 cm square and 6 mm thick on its end (centre 5 cm from the pivot, top 12.9 cm up). Pressing the pad down takes 5.0 N to start and 12.8 N at its stop, 30 degrees (2.5 cm) down, where the jaws are 39.5 mm apart; let go, it springs back up and the jaws close. (5) An empty 100 mL round-bottom flask of borosilicate glass (90 g): a bulb 6.4 cm across and a neck 2.5 cm across ending 8.75 cm above the bulb's middle in a lip 3 cm across and 5 mm tall. It stands in a cork ring (8 cm across, with a 4.5 cm hole, 1.5 cm tall) at 28 cm forward and 17 cm right of the centre line, the top of its lip 12.5 cm up. Clamped 4.2 cm above the bulb's middle, its bottom hangs about 2.1 cm above the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end, except that a drop or a tip counts at any time: 0.0 if the flask was ever dropped (falling faster than 1 m/s) or tipped more than 45 degrees from upright. Clamped: the flask hangs from the clamp by its neck: the neck between the closed jaws (their pads 20 to 30 mm apart, the neck's axis within 7 mm of the jaws' middle line, along their length at least 6 mm in from their front ends, and at their height within 12 mm), the flask upright within 10 degrees and its bottom at least 5 mm above the table. 1.0: clamped, and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre, its TCP, within 5 cm of its start), so both hands have let go; 0.5: clamped, even with a hand still on the flask; 0.25: the neck between the open jaws (pads more than 30 mm apart) at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the flask still. In a real trial, the video shows drops (the flask falling from the hand or the clamp), tips, the neck between the open jaws and the hands off and home; at the end, a side photo with a protractor card behind the flask shows both cork pads on the neck below the lip and the tilt, and a 5 mm gauge block slid under the bulb shows that it hangs.
reset_notes: Press the lever, take the flask out of the jaws and stand it back in its cork ring.
fidelity: Rigid bodies (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the clamp's push rod, wedge and springs are not separate bodies; each jaw is a slider whose spring drive (3 N preload, 250 N/m) follows the wedge position computed from the lever's angle, and the lever's hinge spring carries the jaw springs' load through that linkage (exact at rest and on its stop, within 8% between). The stand is fixed; glass can't break (drops and tips score 0). Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
